current_example.title: Example: Finding the Arc Length of a Polar Curve

q-103831.name: Question 1
q-103831.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14151533/assets/b1a0f5b8438b5abeafafccadd5a3a33572441c4d58d2e97f7254bd28987c223c.png)

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{5\pi }{6}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
q-103831.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}+(-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+144{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{16({cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta ))}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

a

b
4∫π/25π/6cos2⁡(3θ)−sin2⁡(3θ)dθ

EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=4cos⁡(3θ), we have

drdθ=−12sin⁡(3θ).

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫π/25π/6(4cos⁡(3θ))2+(−12sin⁡(3θ))2dθ=∫π/25π/616cos2⁡(3θ)+144sin2⁡(3θ)dθ=∫π/25π/616(cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ))dθ=4∫π/25π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ.

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=3-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above).
q-15129.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(3-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}+(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+1+8{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{10-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+8{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=3−cos⁡(3θ), we have drdθ=3sin⁡(3θ).

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/2(3−cos⁡(3θ))2+(3sin⁡(3θ))2dθ=∫0π/29−6cos⁡(3θ)+cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ=∫0π/29−6cos⁡(3θ)+1+8sin2⁡(3θ)dθ=∫0π/210−6cos⁡(3θ)+8sin2⁡(3θ)dθ.

q-15122.name: Question 3
q-15122.problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $-\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}?$
q-15122.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}+(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+36{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta ))}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=2cos⁡(3θ) for −π6≤θ≤π6?

a
2∫−π/6π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+3sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
b
2∫0π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
c
∫−π/6π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
d
2∫−π/6π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
e
∫0π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+3sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=2cos⁡(3θ), we have drdθ=−6sin⁡(3θ).

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/6π/6(2cos⁡(3θ))2+(−6sin⁡(3θ))2dθ=∫−π/6π/64cos2⁡(3θ)+36sin2⁡(3θ)dθ=∫−π/6π/64(cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ))dθ=2∫−π/6π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ.

q-15121.name: Question 4
q-15121.problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{5}?$
q-15121.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta ))^{2}+(5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(5\theta )+25{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

?

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=sin⁡(5θ) for 0≤θ≤π5?

a
∫0π/5sin2⁡(5θ)+5cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
b
∫0π/5sin2⁡(5θ)+25cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
c
∫0π/5(sin2⁡(5θ)+25cos2⁡(5θ))dθ
d
2∫0π/5(sin⁡(5θ)+5cos⁡(5θ))2dθ
e
2∫0π/5sin⁡(5θ)+5cos⁡(5θ)dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=sin⁡(5θ), we have drdθ=5cos⁡(5θ).

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/5(sin⁡(5θ))2+(5cos⁡(5θ))2dθ=∫0π/5sin2⁡(5θ)+25cos2⁡(5θ)dθ.

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
q-51199.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+1+3{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+3{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

?

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=1+cos⁡(2θ) for −π2≤θ≤π2 (shown in blue in the diagram above)?

a
∫−π/2π/21+2cos⁡(2θ)−3sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
b
∫−π/2π/22+2cos⁡(2θ)dθ
c
∫−π/2π/22−2cos⁡(2θ)dθ
d
∫−π/2π/22+2cos⁡(2θ)+3sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
e
∫−π/2π/21+2cos⁡(2θ)+sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=1+cos⁡(2θ), we have drdθ=−2sin⁡(2θ).

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/2π/2(1+cos⁡(2θ))2+(−2sin⁡(2θ))2dθ=∫−π/2π/21+2cos⁡(2θ)+cos2⁡(2θ)+4sin2⁡(2θ)dθ=∫−π/2π/21+2cos⁡(2θ)+1+3sin2⁡(2θ)dθ=∫−π/2π/22+2cos⁡(2θ)+3sin2⁡(2θ)dθ.

q-103848.name: Question 6
q-103848.problem: Find the arc length of the polar curve $r={4}^{\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
q-103848.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={4}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }={4}^{\theta }\operatorname{ln}⁡4.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({4}^{\theta })}^{2}+{({4}^{\theta }\operatorname{ln}⁡4)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{4}^{2\theta }+{4}^{2\theta }{ln}^{2}⁡4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(1+{ln}^{2}⁡4){4}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{1+{ln}^{2}⁡4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{4}^{\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{1+{ln}^{2}⁡4}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\cdot {4}^{\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{ln}^{2}⁡4}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\cdot ({4}^{\pi /2}-{4}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{1+{ln}^{2}⁡4}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}({4}^{\pi /2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$
